CHAPTER 1 — THE SYSTEM AT A GLANCE
The Ninja Creami XL Deluxe (NC501 series) is not a churner and not a blender. In the Master
Architecture’s terms it is a precision vertical lathe: an 800-watt motor drives a dual-stage
paddle down into a completely frozen solid block at roughly 1,800 RPM, micro-shaving
microscopically thin layers off the frozen cylinder. Conventional ice cream leans on 14–20%
butterfat and 15–22% sucrose to stay soft; a no-added-sugar, ~80 g-protein block instead
freezes like a crystalline polymer — which is why surface geometry, stabilizer load and freeze
discipline are hardware-protection issues, not culinary preferences.
The method is a 7-step pipeline in three phases, executed
in strict order. Total fluid per pint: 600–645 g (21.2–22.8
oz) in a 24 oz (709 mL) tub, never past the Max Fill line.

Step 2 · Thermal emulsion vortex
Dissolve the bone broth (1 scoop · ~10 g) and collagen (1

Step 4 · Stratified lid-off freezing — owner
canon
Freeze the tub uncovered for the first 2–4 hours at −18 °C to
−20 °C (0 °F to −4 °F): unrestricted vertical expansion prevents the centre dome from ever
forming. Snap the lid on and freeze undisturbed to a total of 24 hours (16 hours absolute

D O C U M E N T E D D I V E R G E N C E — O W N E R C A N O N
Ninja’s manual instructs freezing with the lid snapped on for 24 hours. The lid-off first
phase is established community technique (Tasty Travelers, Kroll’s Korner) adopted as
owner canon in this system because it prevents the hump at the source. It is labelled
wherever it appears (Chapter 11, Claim 3) and never presented as manufacturer
guidance.
Step 5 · Masher levelling & perimeter bath
Solid-block check: the pint must be 100% frozen solid.
Any soft centre → back to the freezer for 4 hours.
Perimeter bath: warm tap water over the lower half of the
tub’s outer walls for 30–60 seconds — never past 60 s.
Levelling: press the Deiss stainless masher straight down,
firmly, shattering any frost peak into a perfectly horizontal
plane. Never twist — tub walls crack.
Step 6 · Mechanical processing & re-spin
tuning
Lock the tub into the outer bowl, selector to Full, program Lite
Ice Cream — or Sorbet for pure isolate bases, whose higher
shear duration suits dense isolate matrices. Never standard Ice
Cream on these bases (Chapter 11, Claim 4). After the first
spin:
Wall scrape: run a butter knife gently around the inner
wall — the paddle leaves a ~1 mm (0.04 in) frost ring it
cannot reach — and fold those crystals into the core. Gentle pressure; the manual cautions
against aggressive metal utensils in the pint.
Dry re-spin first: for hard-scoop gelato density, re-spin with no added liquid; blade
friction binds the mass. This is Ninja’s own NC501 procedure (Claim 5).

CHAPTER 8 — THE PHYSICS & FOOD SCIENCE OF
THE BASE
Hydrophobicity and stabilization
Protein isolates resist water integration. Dry protein or gum dropped straight into liquid forms
hydrophobic “glue pockets” that freeze into icy lumps and load the paddle with dangerous
resistance. Hence the system’s first law: stabilizer is always isolated inside the dry matrix
before liquid appears (Step 1), then streamed into a moving vortex (Step 2). Gum
manufacturers prescribe the identical technique — pre-blend with dry powders to prevent
“fish-eye” clumps (Chapter 11, Claim 7).
Volumetric expansion and the centre hump
Egg-white albumin and whey trap micro-air during blending and give the base its overrun —
but frozen under a sealed lid, that expansion drives the centre upward into a frost hump. A
convex surface deflects the descending spindle and loads the drive with lateral shear. The
countermeasures are layered: the 15-minute settle, the lid-off first freeze phase, and masher
levelling before any spin. Ninja’s manual forbids processing a pint frozen unevenly or at an
angle; the hump itself is documented in community forensic practice (Chapter 11, Claim 2).
Freezing-point depression — the allulose engine
Freezing-point depression is colligative: it scales with the number of dissolved particles, not
their mass. Allulose (molecular weight 180.16 g/mol) delivers nearly twice the particle count
per gram of sucrose (342.3 g/mol) — a freezing-point depression factor of 1.9×. The system’s
dose of 25–35 g (0.9–1.2 oz) of crystalline allulose per pint therefore softens the frozen
matrix measurably, without the crystallization-in-storage that hardens erythritol-sweetened
pints, and without sugar. Published references confirm allulose depresses the freezing point
and supports scoopability (Chapter 11, Claim 9), with the nuance recorded there.
The hydrocolloid anti-slime law
Xanthan, guar and tara are pseudoplastic, shear-thinning hydrocolloids. In a plain isolate base
they suppress ice crystals cleanly at 1/4 tsp (1.0 g · 1000 mg). But in matrices that already
carry whey/casein blends and modified starches (instant pudding mixes), total hydrocolloid
load above roughly 0.25% w/w cross-links into an elastic, rubbery slime. That threshold is the
physical basis of the calibration rule in Chapter 2: blends and pudding bases are halved to 1/8
tsp (0.5 g · 500 mg).
The taste-audit law
Sub-zero temperatures temporarily anesthetize taste receptors: cold dulls sweetness and
flavour. The warm base must therefore taste noticeably over-sweet at the pre-freeze audit; a

What the collagen is — and is not

GELITA’s technical data they cannot form a gel network at any useful concentration. In this
system, bone broth and marine collagen are a protein payload — amino acids and macro
